t: Populism has no single agreed definition: scholars treat it as a thin-centred ideology, a class phenomenon, a discursive logic, a political style, a strategy for winning power or a pattern of economic policy, and some have proposed abandoning the word.

The word first appeared in English in 1858 and took hold through the United States People's Party of the 1880s to early 1900s, while the Russian narodniki of the 1860s and 1870s, often translated as populists, differed from it in ideology and course.

Scholars sharply disagree on its relation to democracy: some define it as inherently anti-democratic, others as a democratic impulse that empowers marginalised groups, and others hold that it takes contradictory forms depending on context.
dyk: Between 1950 and 1960 roughly 160 publications on populism were recorded, and by 2018 the number of academic papers and books with the term in their title or abstract had grown to 615 in a single year; the Cambridge Dictionary chose "populism" as its Word of the Year in 2017.
ev: The word "populist" first appears in English, as an antonym for "aristocratic" in a translation of a work by Alphonse de Lamartine
The National People's Party adopts its first national platform in the United States, which calls for protecting the rights of urban workmen
The People's Party supports the Democratic candidate William Jennings Bryan, and its support plunges after his defeat
Léon Lemonnier publishes a manifesto for the populist novel in France
The mass mobilisation of 17 October in Argentina, often considered the founding moment of Peronism
Edward Shils in the United States and Hélio Jaguaribe in Brazil publish the texts that turn populism into an academic concept
A conference at the London School of Economics fails to produce a unified theory of populism
The election of Donald Trump and the United Kingdom's vote to leave the European Union are widely read as expressions of populist sentiment

f.thinkers: Hélio Jaguaribe, whose 1954 text is considered the first academic study of Latin American populism; Edward Shils, who proposed populism in 1954 as a term for anti-elite trends in US society; Richard Hofstadter and Daniel Bell, who read the People's Party as status anxiety; Gino Germani and Seymour Martin Lipset, on mass mobilisation; Ernesto Laclau of the Essex School, who treats populism as a discursive logic; Cas Mudde and Cristóbal Rovira Kaltwasser, who call it a thin-centred ideology; Kurt Weyland, who defines it as a political strategy
f.texts: Léon Lemonnier's 1929 manifesto of the populist novel; the National People's Party's first national platform of 1892; Hélio Jaguaribe's 1954 study of Latin American populism; Edward Shils's 1954 article on anti-elite trends in the United States
f.ideas: a society divided between the pure people and a corrupt elite; the general will of the people; the common sense of the people set above expert and institutional knowledge; distrust of representative institutions and a preference for direct decisions such as referendums; a charismatic leader as the voice of the people; a style of politics that breaks with the manners of the established elite
f.today: The term is applied to parties and leaders on both left and right, among them Greece's Syriza, Spain's Podemos, India's Aam Aadmi Party, Austria's Freedom Party, the Swiss People's Party and Argentina's Justicialist Party, and scholars still disagree over whether it is a useful category at all
